notes:
Wave basics

  • Wave equation: $y=A\sin(\omega t - kx)$; $v=f\lambda$; $\omega=2\pi f$; wave number $k=2\pi/\lambda$.
  • Transverse wave: particle motion $\perp$ wave propagation (e.g. wave on a string, light). Longitudinal wave: particle motion $\parallel$ propagation (e.g. sound).

Speed of waves

MediumSpeed formula
Stretched string$v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$ ($T$ = tension, $\mu$ = mass per unit length)
Sound in gas (Newton-Laplace)$v=\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$; speed increases with temperature, $v\propto\sqrt T_{abs}$
Sound in solid$v=\sqrt{Y/\rho}$ (Young's modulus $Y$)
  • Speed of sound in air at a given pressure is independent of pressure (since $P/\rho$ constant at fixed $T$) but increases with humidity (moist air is less dense) and temperature.

Superposition, reflection & standing waves

  • Principle of superposition: resultant displacement = algebraic sum of individual displacements.
  • Standing (stationary) waves form by superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; nodes (zero displacement) and antinodes (max displacement) are fixed in space, spaced $\lambda/4$ apart alternately (adjacent nodes/antinodes are $\lambda/2$ apart).

Vibrations of strings & air columns

SystemFundamental frequencyHarmonics present
Stretched string (both ends fixed)$f_1=\dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}$all harmonics $f_n=nf_1$
Open organ pipe (both ends open)$f_1=\dfrac{v}{2L}$all harmonics $nf_1$
Closed organ pipe (one end closed)$f_1=\dfrac{v}{4L}$only odd harmonics $(2n-1)f_1$

Beats & Doppler effect

  • Beats: two sources of close frequencies $f_1,f_2$ produce beat frequency $|f_1-f_2|$.
  • Doppler effect (sound), observer/source moving along the line joining them: $f' = f\left(\dfrac{v\pm v_o}{v\mp v_s}\right)$ — use $+v_o$ if observer approaches source, $-v_s$ if source approaches observer (apparent frequency increases as source/observer approach each other, decreases as they recede).

Exam tip

KCET typically asks 2-3 questions from this chapter, commonly on organ pipe/string harmonics, beat frequency, or Doppler effect numericals. Memorise that a closed pipe supports only odd harmonics and its fundamental is half that of an open pipe of the same length.

questions.q: A wave is represented by $y=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$. Its speed of propagation is given by
questions.explanation: Wave speed $v=f\lambda=\dfrac{\omega/2\pi}{2\pi/k}\times2\pi=\omega/k$.
questions.trick: Wave speed $v=\omega/k$ — coefficient of $t$ over coefficient of $x$.

questions.q: Sound waves travelling through air are
questions.explanation: In sound waves, air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation, making them longitudinal waves.
questions.trick: Sound: particles vibrate along propagation direction $\Rightarrow$ longitudinal wave.

questions.q: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string of tension $T$ and mass per unit length $\mu$ is
questions.explanation: $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$ is the standard formula for wave speed on a stretched string.
questions.trick: Memorise string wave speed formula: $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$.

questions.q: If the tension in a stretched string is made 4 times (mass per unit length unchanged), the speed of transverse waves on it becomes
questions.explanation: $v\propto\sqrt T$; quadrupling $T$ doubles $v$.
questions.trick: $v\propto\sqrt T$ — quadrupling tension only doubles the speed.

questions.q: The speed of sound in a gas increases with
options: increase in density at constant temperature and pressure
increase in pressure at constant temperature
questions.explanation: $v=\sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$, so $v \propto \sqrt T$; speed of sound in a gas increases with absolute temperature and is independent of pressure at constant temperature.
questions.trick: $v\propto\sqrt T_{abs}$ for sound in gas — higher temperature, faster sound.

questions.q: Two adjacent nodes in a stationary wave are separated by a distance of
questions.explanation: In a stationary wave, adjacent nodes (and adjacent antinodes) are separated by $\lambda/2$; a node and the next antinode are separated by $\lambda/4$.
questions.trick: Adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart; node-to-antinode is $\lambda/4$.

questions.q: A closed organ pipe of length $L$ has fundamental frequency $f$. An open organ pipe of the same length has fundamental frequency
questions.explanation: Closed pipe: $f=v/4L$. Open pipe of same length: $f_{open}=v/2L=2f$.
questions.trick: Closed pipe $f=v/4L$; open pipe same $L$ gives $f_{open}=v/2L=2f$.

questions.q: A closed organ pipe can resonate at frequencies in the ratio
questions.explanation: A closed pipe (one end closed) supports only odd harmonics of its fundamental: $f_1:f_3:f_5=1:3:5...$
questions.trick: Closed pipe: only odd harmonics, ratio $1:3:5:7\ldots$ — memorise.

questions.q: A string of length 1 m, fixed at both ends, vibrates in its fundamental mode with frequency 100 Hz. The speed of transverse waves on the string is
questions.explanation: Fundamental: $f_1=v/2L \Rightarrow v=2Lf_1=2\times1\times100=200$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Fixed-fixed string fundamental: $v=2Lf_1$ — rearrange and plug directly.

questions.q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats heard per second is
questions.explanation: Beat frequency $=|f_1-f_2|=|260-256|=4$ Hz.
questions.trick: Beat frequency $=|f_1-f_2|$ — simple subtraction, no formula needed.

questions.q: A tuning fork of unknown frequency produces 4 beats per second with a standard fork of frequency 256 Hz. When the unknown fork is loaded with wax, the beat frequency decreases. The frequency of the unknown fork is
questions.explanation: Loading with wax decreases the unknown fork's frequency. Since the beat frequency decreased, the unknown frequency must have been above 256 Hz, moving closer to it: $f=256+4=260$ Hz.
questions.trick: Wax lowers frequency; beats decreasing means unknown was above standard: add 4.

questions.q: A source of sound of frequency 500 Hz moves towards a stationary observer with a speed of 34 m s$^{-1}$. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s$^{-1}$, the apparent frequency heard by the observer is
questions.explanation: $f'=f\dfrac{v}{v-v_s}=500\times\dfrac{340}{340-34}=500\times\dfrac{340}{306}\approx556$ Hz.
questions.trick: Source approaching: $f'=f\cdot v/(v-v_s)$ — denominator shrinks, frequency rises.

questions.q: An observer moves towards a stationary source of sound with speed $v_o$. The apparent frequency heard is
questions.explanation: When the observer approaches a stationary source, apparent frequency $f'=f\dfrac{v+v_o}{v}$, which is greater than $f$.
questions.trick: Observer approaching stationary source: $f'=f(v+v_o)/v$ — numerator grows.

questions.q: The Doppler effect in sound shows an apparent change in
options: wavelength of sound in the medium only, not frequency
frequency heard by the observer due to relative motion between source and observer
questions.explanation: The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency (and wavelength) of a wave observed due to relative motion between the source and the observer.
questions.trick: Doppler effect = apparent frequency shift from relative source-observer motion.

questions.q: The fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe of length $L$ is $f_1$. The frequency of its first overtone is
questions.explanation: An open pipe supports all harmonics $nf_1$; the first overtone is the second harmonic, $2f_1$.
questions.trick: Open pipe harmonics are all integers $nf_1$; first overtone $=2f_1$.

questions.q: The fundamental frequency of a closed organ pipe is $f_1$. Its first overtone (next resonant frequency above fundamental) is
questions.explanation: A closed pipe supports only odd harmonics $f_1,3f_1,5f_1,...$; its first overtone is the third harmonic, $3f_1$.
questions.trick: Closed pipe: only odd harmonics $\Rightarrow$ first overtone is $3f_1$, not $2f_1$.

questions.q: Two waves of equal amplitude $a$ and same frequency, differing in phase by $\pi$ (180°), superpose. The resultant amplitude is
questions.explanation: For phase difference $\pi$, the waves destructively interfere completely (for equal amplitudes): resultant amplitude $=\sqrt{a^2+a^2+2a^2\cos\pi}=0$.
questions.trick: Phase $\pi$, equal amplitude $\Rightarrow$ perfect cancellation, resultant amplitude zero.

questions.q: In a stationary wave pattern, the points of zero displacement at all times are called
questions.explanation: Nodes are points of permanent zero displacement in a stationary wave; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude of vibration.
questions.trick: Nodes = permanent zero displacement; antinodes = maximum displacement points.

questions.q: A sound wave has frequency 170 Hz and wavelength 2 m. Its speed is
questions.explanation: $v=f\lambda=170\times2=340$ m/s.
questions.trick: $v=f\lambda$ — direct multiplication, no other formula needed.

questions.q: A transverse wave is represented by $y=A\sin(\omega t+kx)$. It travels along the
options: it is a standing wave, not travelling
questions.explanation: For $y=A\sin(\omega t+kx)$, a point of constant phase requires $x$ to decrease as $t$ increases, so the wave travels in the negative x-direction (opposite to $y=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$, which travels in $+x$).
questions.trick: $\sin(\omega t+kx)$ form travels in $-x$; $(\omega t-kx)$ travels in $+x$.

questions.q: A transverse wave pulse on a string reflects from a rigid (fixed) end. The reflected pulse undergoes a phase change of
questions.explanation: Reflection at a rigid boundary inverts the pulse, a phase reversal of $\pi$; reflection at a free end occurs with no phase change.
questions.trick: Fixed-end reflection inverts the pulse $\Rightarrow$ phase change of $\pi$.

questions.q: The principle of superposition of waves states that when two or more waves overlap at a point, the resultant displacement is
options: equal to the displacement of the larger wave only
the algebraic sum of the displacements due to each wave separately
the product of the individual displacements
questions.explanation: By the principle of superposition, the net displacement at a point is the vector (here, algebraic) sum of the individual displacements due to each wave.
questions.trick: Superposition: net displacement is just the algebraic sum of individual waves.

questions.q: Superposition of two waves $y_1=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$ and $y_2=A\sin(\omega t+kx)$ produces a stationary wave given by
questions.explanation: Expanding: $\sin(\omega t-kx)+\sin(\omega t+kx)=2\sin\omega t\cos kx$, so $y=2A\sin\omega t\cos kx$: an amplitude $2A\cos kx$ fixed in space, oscillating in time as $\sin\omega t$ — a stationary wave.
questions.trick: Opposite-direction waves combine to $2A\sin\omega t\cos kx$ — standing wave form.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic. The total number of nodes (including the two fixed ends) is
questions.explanation: The $n$th harmonic of a string fixed at both ends has $(n+1)$ nodes and $n$ antinodes; for $n=3$, nodes $=4$.
questions.trick: $n$th harmonic of fixed-fixed string has $(n+1)$ nodes — third harmonic gives 4.

questions.q: In a resonance tube experiment with a tuning fork of frequency 500 Hz, the first and second resonance lengths of the air column are 16 cm and 50 cm. The speed of sound in air is
questions.explanation: $\lambda/2 = l_2-l_1 = 50-16=34$ cm $\Rightarrow \lambda=68$ cm $=0.68$ m; $v=f\lambda=500\times0.68=340$ m/s.
questions.trick: Resonance tube: $\lambda/2=l_2-l_1$, then $v=f\lambda$ — classic two-step.

questions.q: The pitch of a musical sound is primarily determined by its
questions.explanation: Pitch, the perceived highness or lowness of a note, corresponds to the frequency of the sound wave.
questions.trick: Pitch $\leftrightarrow$ frequency; loudness $\leftrightarrow$ amplitude/intensity — don't confuse them.

questions.q: The loudness of a sound is mainly determined by its
questions.explanation: Loudness is a physiological sensation corresponding to the intensity of the sound wave, which depends on its amplitude.
questions.trick: Loudness tracks intensity (amplitude squared), not frequency or wavelength.

questions.q: Two notes of the same frequency and loudness, played on a sitar and a flute, sound different. This difference is attributed to their
options: quality (timbre), due to different harmonic content
questions.explanation: Quality (timbre) distinguishes sounds of the same pitch and loudness and arises from the different combination of harmonics (overtones) present.
questions.trick: Same pitch and loudness but different sound $=$ quality/timbre from harmonic mix.

questions.q: The audible range of frequencies for a normal human ear is approximately
questions.explanation: The normal human ear can perceive sound frequencies roughly from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
questions.trick: Memorise the audible range: 20 Hz to 20 kHz for the human ear.

questions.q: Sound waves with frequency greater than 20 kHz, inaudible to the human ear, are called
questions.explanation: Waves above the upper audible limit (20 kHz) are called ultrasonic waves.
questions.trick: Above 20 kHz (inaudible, high) = ultrasonic; below 20 Hz = infrasonic.

questions.q: Sound waves of frequency below 20 Hz are called
questions.explanation: Waves below the lower audible limit (20 Hz) are called infrasonic waves.
questions.trick: Below 20 Hz (inaudible, low) = infrasonic; above 20 kHz = ultrasonic.

questions.q: If the amplitude of a wave is doubled, keeping its frequency constant, its intensity becomes
questions.explanation: Intensity $I\propto A^2$ (for fixed frequency and medium), so doubling amplitude quadruples the intensity.
questions.trick: Intensity $I\propto A^2$ — doubling amplitude quadruples intensity, not doubles.

questions.q: A source of sound (frequency $f$) and an observer move directly towards each other, source with speed $v_s$ and observer with speed $v_o$, in a medium where sound speed is $v$. The apparent frequency heard is
questions.explanation: When both approach each other, the observer term takes $+v_o$ and the source term takes $-v_s$, both increasing the apparent frequency: $f'=f\dfrac{v+v_o}{v-v_s}$.
questions.trick: Both approach: observer term $+v_o$ (numerator), source term $-v_s$ (denominator).

questions.q: Two points on a wave have a path difference of $\lambda/4$. The corresponding phase difference between them is
questions.explanation: Phase difference $\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
questions.trick: Phase diff $=(2\pi/\lambda)\times$path diff — plug $\lambda/4$ directly for $\pi/2$.

questions.q: Two coherent waves interfere constructively at a point when their path difference is
questions.explanation: Constructive interference occurs when the path difference is an integral (whole number) multiple of the wavelength, $n\lambda$.
questions.trick: Constructive interference: path difference $=$ integral multiple of $\lambda$ ($n\lambda$).

questions.q: Two coherent waves of equal amplitude interfere destructively (cancel completely) at a point when their path difference is
questions.explanation: Destructive interference (for equal amplitudes, complete cancellation) occurs when the path difference is an odd multiple of half the wavelength, $(2n-1)\lambda/2$.
questions.trick: Destructive (equal amplitude) interference: path difference $=$ odd multiple of $\lambda/2$.

questions.q: In a sonometer experiment, keeping the vibrating length and mass per unit length constant, if the tension in the wire is made 4 times, the frequency of vibration becomes
questions.explanation: $f=\dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}\propto\sqrt T$; quadrupling $T$ doubles $f$.
questions.trick: Sonometer: $f\propto\sqrt T$ — quadrupling tension only doubles frequency.

questions.q: Two wires of the same material and under the same tension have the same length, but their radii are in the ratio 1:2. The ratio of their fundamental frequencies is
questions.explanation: $\mu=\rho\pi r^2$, so for the same $L,T,\rho$: $f\propto1/\sqrt\mu\propto1/r$; with $r_1:r_2=1:2$, $f_1:f_2=2:1$.
questions.trick: $\mu\propto r^2\Rightarrow f\propto1/r$ (same $L,T$) — thinner wire, higher frequency.

questions.q: The SI unit of frequency of a wave is
questions.explanation: Frequency, the number of oscillations per second, is measured in hertz (Hz).
questions.trick: Frequency's SI unit is always hertz (Hz), oscillations per second.

questions.q: An open organ pipe and a closed organ pipe have the same fundamental frequency. The length of the closed pipe compared to the open pipe is
questions.explanation: $f_{open}=v/2L_{open}$ and $f_{closed}=v/4L_{closed}$. Equating: $L_{closed}=L_{open}/2$, so the closed pipe is half as long as the open pipe of equal fundamental frequency.
questions.trick: Equal fundamentals: $v/2L_{open}=v/4L_{closed}\Rightarrow L_{closed}=L_{open}/2$.
